passages.t: Bad shepherds, and a righteous Branch for David
passages.happening:
“Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of My pasture!” (verse 1). The shepherds of God's people have scattered the flock and not cared for it, so God will attend to them for their evil (verse 2). ‘Then I Myself will gather the remnant of My flock from all the lands to which I have banished them’ (verse 3). He will bring them back to their pasture, and raise up shepherds who will care for them, so that none will be afraid or missing (verse 4).

‘Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and He will reign wisely as King and will administer justice and righteousness in the land’ (verse 5). ‘In His days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell securely’ (verse 6). His name will be ‘The LORD Our Righteousness’ (verse 6).

People will no longer swear by the God who brought Israel out of Egypt, but by the God who brought them back from the land of the north and all the lands where he scattered them (verses 7 and 8).
passages.hearers:
Across the ancient Near East, kings called themselves shepherds of their people, and David had been a shepherd boy. So the shepherds here are the rulers. A good shepherd kept the flock together and protected it. Judah's kings had scattered theirs.

The last king was Zedekiah, put on the throne by Nebuchadnezzar in 597 BC. His name means roughly that the LORD is his righteousness. The name of the coming king in verse 6 takes Zedekiah's name and gives it to a better king. The first hearers would hear the play: the man who carried the name did not live up to it; the Branch would.

A branch, or shoot, grows from a stump. David's family tree was about to be cut down. God promises a new shoot from its root.

Verses 7 and 8 repeat the promise of a new exodus from 16:14-15.
passages.later: Zechariah, after the return, hears God promise ‘My servant, the Branch’ (Zechariah 3:8). Ezekiel promises ‘one shepherd, My servant David’ (Ezekiel 34:23). Christians have long seen this king in Jesus, the son of David.
passages.asks: God promises shepherds who will care for the flock so that none goes missing. Ask whom you are responsible for, and whether you scatter or gather them. And ask what it means that God himself will gather the remnant when its leaders fail.

passages.happening:
‘As for the prophets: My heart is broken within me, and all my bones tremble’ (verse 9). Jeremiah is like a drunk man because of the LORD and his holy words. The land is full of adulterers, and the pastures dry up (verse 10). ‘For both prophet and priest are ungodly; even in My house I have found their wickedness’ (verse 11).

Among the prophets of Samaria God saw an offensive thing: they prophesied by Baal (verse 13). Among the prophets of Jerusalem he has seen something worse: ‘They commit adultery and walk in lies. They strengthen the hands of evildoers’ (verse 14), so that no one turns from wickedness.

The people must not listen to them. They fill people with false hopes and speak visions from their own minds (verse 16). They keep telling those who despise God that they will have peace (verse 17). ‘But which of them has stood in the council of the LORD to see and hear His word?’ (verse 18). ‘I did not send these prophets, yet they have run with their message’ (verse 21). If they had stood in God's council, they would have turned the people from their evil ways (verse 22).

‘Am I only a God nearby,’ declares the LORD, ‘and not a God far away?’ (verse 23). ‘Do I not fill the heavens and the earth?’ (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
The prophets in view were real public figures, often attached to the temple and the royal court. They reassured the nation that Babylon would not win and that Jerusalem, as the LORD's city, was safe.

Verse 13 looks back to the northern kingdom, whose capital Samaria fell to Assyria in 722 BC. Its prophets had spoken in the name of Baal. Jerusalem's prophets used the LORD's name, but their lives and their message made them worse.

The council of the LORD was the picture of God's heavenly court, where a true prophet stood to hear what God had decided. The false prophets had never been there. They spoke from their own minds.

A God nearby could be managed and kept close to the temple. A God who fills heaven and earth sees everything, including the lies spoken in his name.
passages.later: The law gave one test of a prophet: ‘When a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD and the message does not come to pass’, it is not God's word (Deuteronomy 18:22). A psalm asks, ‘Where can I flee from Your presence?’ (Psalm 139:7).
passages.hard:
If both true and false prophets said the LORD declares, how was anyone supposed to tell the difference?

It was truly hard, which is why the book spends so much time on it. Deuteronomy 18:21-22 offers one test, whether the word comes to pass, but that could only be applied afterward. Jeremiah adds tests that could be applied at the time. A true prophet stands in the LORD's council and so speaks in line with what God has already revealed in his covenant; the false prophets promise peace to people who despise the LORD (verse 17). A true word calls people to turn from their evil ways (verse 22), while a false one strengthens the hands of evildoers (verse 14). The prophet's own life matters too: verse 14 charges them with adultery and lies.

None of this made the choice easy for people living through it, and chapter 28 shows two prophets facing each other in the temple with opposite messages. But the tests are not arbitrary: agreement with God's revealed character, a call to repentance, and a life that matches the message.
passages.asks: The false prophets told people who despised God that all would be well. Ask which voices you listen to because they never call you to turn. And ask whether your own life matches what you say about God.

passages.t: Straw and grain, fire and hammer
passages.happening:
God has heard the prophets who prophesy lies in his name, saying they have had a dream (verse 25). How long will this go on in the hearts of prophets who prophesy the delusions of their own minds (verse 26)? Their dreams make God's people forget his name, as their fathers forgot it through Baal (verse 27).

‘Let the prophet who has a dream retell it, but let him who has My word speak it truthfully. For what is straw compared to grain?’ (verse 28). God asks whether his word is not like fire, and like a hammer that smashes a rock (verse 29). He is against the prophets who steal words from one another and claim they are his (verse 30), who wag their own tongues and say the LORD declares it (verse 31), and who lead his people astray with false dreams and reckless lies (verse 32).

The chapter ends with a play on the word burden. When people ask what the burden of the LORD is, Jeremiah is to say that they are the burden, and God will cast them off (verse 33). No one is to speak of the burden of the LORD any more, for each man's own word has become his burden; they are to ask simply what the LORD has answered and spoken (verses 34 to 40).
passages.hearers:
Dreams were a known way of receiving messages in the ancient world, and the Bible itself records God speaking in dreams. The problem was not dreaming but passing off one's own dreams as God's word.

Straw and grain came together on the threshing floor, and the work of threshing was to separate them. The straw was light and useless; the grain was food. God's word has weight and nourishes. The false prophets' words were straw.

The word for burden, massa, also meant an oracle, a weighty word from God. People asked Jeremiah mockingly for the latest burden. God turns the word around: the people themselves have become the burden he will throw down. Then he forbids the phrase altogether, because it had been so cheapened.
passages.later: Hebrews says the same of God's word: ‘For the word of God is living and active. Sharper than any double-edged sword’ (Hebrews 4:12). The law's test stood behind all of this (Deuteronomy 18:22).
passages.asks: God's word is like fire and a hammer that breaks rock. Ask whether you have let God's word break anything in you, or only comfort you. And ask whether you have ever passed off your own opinions as what God says.
